ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure shows a common-emitter transistor amplifier circuit. The emitter is directly grounded; the collector is connected to the 12 V power supply through a 1 kΩ resistor; the right side of the collector node is labeled with the output/collector voltage vc, with polarity positive at the top and negative at the bottom. The collector node is also fed back to the base through a 53 kΩ resistor. The input source vs is connected to the base through 5.3 kΩ and the coupling capacitor Cc. The problem states that Cc can be considered infinitely large, but when doing DC bias analysis, the input coupling branch does not affect the base DC bias. Then reason: Since the emitter is grounded and VBE = 0.7 V, the base voltage is approximately 0.7 V in DC. Let the collector voltage be VC; since the emitter is 0 V, VCE = VC. The base current is provided from the collector through the 53 kΩ feedback resistor: IB = (VC - 0.7)/53 kΩ. The current in the collector 1 kΩ resistor is IC + IB = (β + 1)IB, therefore VC = 12 - 1 kΩ·(β + 1)(VC - 0.7)/53 kΩ. When β = 60, VC = 12 - (61/53)(VC - 0.7), solving gives VC ≈ 5.95 V, namely VCE ≈ 5.95 V. When β increases by 10%, β = 66, VC = 12 - (67/53)(VC - 0.7), solving gives VC ≈ 5.69 V, namely VCE ≈ 5.69 V. VCE decreases from about 5.95 V to about 5.69 V, and the decrease ratio is about (5.95 - 5.69)/5.95 ≈ 4.4%, less than 10%. Therefore the collector-to-emitter voltage drop will decrease, and the decrease will not exceed 10%.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
First describe the image: The figure shows a common-emitter transistor amplifier circuit. The emitter is directly grounded; the collector is connected to the 12 V power supply through a 1 kΩ resistor; the right side of the collector node is labeled with the output/collector voltage vc, with polarity positive at the top and negative at the bottom. The collector node is also fed back to the base through a 53 kΩ resistor. The input source vs is connected to the base through 5.3 kΩ and the coupling capacitor Cc. The problem states that Cc can be considered infinitely large, but when doing DC bias analysis, the input coupling branch does not affect the base DC bias.

Then reason: Since the emitter is grounded and VBE = 0.7 V, the base voltage is approximately 0.7 V in DC. Let the collector voltage be VC; since the emitter is 0 V, VCE = VC. The base current is provided from the collector through the 53 kΩ feedback resistor: IB = (VC - 0.7)/53 kΩ. The current in the collector 1 kΩ resistor is IC + IB = (β + 1)IB, therefore VC = 12 - 1 kΩ·(β + 1)(VC - 0.7)/53 kΩ.

When β = 60, VC = 12 - (61/53)(VC - 0.7), solving gives VC ≈ 5.95 V, namely VCE ≈ 5.95 V. When β increases by 10%, β = 66, VC = 12 - (67/53)(VC - 0.7), solving gives VC ≈ 5.69 V, namely VCE ≈ 5.69 V. VCE decreases from about 5.95 V to about 5.69 V, and the decrease ratio is about (5.95 - 5.69)/5.95 ≈ 4.4%, less than 10%. Therefore the collector-to-emitter voltage drop will decrease, and the decrease will not exceed 10%.
